title: Stacks, Queues, Deques, and Priority Queues
summary: Use std::stack, std::queue, std::deque, and std::priority_queue for last-in-first-out, first-in-first-out, and largest-first work.
intro: Many problems only touch the ends of a collection: undo the last action, serve the next customer, grab the most urgent task. The standard library has a container for each: `std::stack`, `std::queue`, `std::deque`, and `std::priority_queue`. Each one offers only the operations its job needs, so your code says exactly what it does.

steps.title: std::stack: last in, first out

example.title: Reverse a word and check brackets
example.prompt: Push the letters of `drawer` onto a stack, print the size and the top, pop them all to reverse the word, then check two bracket strings.
example.explanation: Pushing the six letters of `drawer` leaves `r`, the last one pushed, on top. The while loop copies the top into `c`, pops, and appends, so the letters come out newest first and spell `reward`. In `{[()]}` every closer meets its own opener on top. In `{[(])}` the `]` arrives while `(` is on top, so `isBalanced` returns false right away. The final `openers.empty()` catches strings like `((` that never close.

practice.title: Reverse stack and check brackets
practice.prompt:
Reverse the word `stack` with a stack, then check two bracket strings.

1. Push each character of `word` onto a `std::stack<char>`.
2. Print the size, then the top, each on its own line.
3. Pop every character, copying the top before each pop, to build the reversed word, and print it.
4. Finish `isBalanced`: push each opener, and on each closer return false if the stack is empty or its top is not the matching opener. Return true only if the stack ends empty.

Expected output:

```text
5
k
kcats
balanced
not balanced
```
hints: Reversing works exactly like the example: while the stack is not empty, copy the top, pop, and append the copy.
In `isBalanced`, a closer is wrong when `c == ')' && open != '('`, and the same for `]` and `}`.
After the loop, leftover openers mean some bracket never closed, so return `openers.empty()`.

steps.title: std::queue: first in, first out
steps.body:
A `std::queue<T>` from `<queue>` is first in, first out, like a line at a counter. You `push` at the back and take from the front. Only the two ends are visible: there is no indexing and no range-for loop.

```cpp
std::queue<std::string> line;
line.push("ana");                   // joins at the back
line.push("ben");
std::cout << line.front() << '\n';  // ana, next to be served
std::cout << line.back() << '\n';   // ben, the newest arrival
line.pop();                         // removes ana
std::cout << line.size() << '\n';   // 1
```

As with `std::stack`, `pop()` returns `void`, and `front()` returns a reference to an element that `pop()` destroys. So copy it first, with `std::string job = q.front();`, then pop. `front`, `back`, and `pop` on an empty queue are undefined behavior, so loop with `while (!q.empty())`.

Processing a queue means taking items in the order they arrived. To retry an item, push the copy you made onto the back again: it waits behind everyone already in line. Use a flag or counter so an item is not re-queued forever.

example.title: Print jobs with one retry
example.prompt: Process three print jobs in arrival order, sending `b.doc` to the back once.
example.output:
3
a.pdf c.png
Printing a.pdf
Retry b.doc
Printing c.png
Printing b.doc
example.explanation: After three pushes `front()` is the first job and `back()` the last. Each pass copies the front into `job` before `pop()`, so `job` stays valid after the element is gone. The first time `b.doc` comes up, `retried` is false, so it is pushed onto the back behind `c.png`. That is why `c.png` prints before `b.doc`. The second time, `retried` is true and it prints normally, and the loop ends when the queue is empty.

practice.title: Customer line
practice.prompt:
Serve a line of customers in arrival order, sending Lee to the back once.

1. Push `Ana`, `Lee`, and `Max` onto `customers`.
2. Print the size on one line, then the front and back on the next line, separated by a space.
3. While the queue is not empty, copy the front into a `std::string` and pop it.
4. The first time you get `Lee`, print `Lee to the back` and push Lee again. Otherwise print `Serving NAME`.

Expected output:

```text
3
Ana Max
Serving Ana
Lee to the back
Serving Max
Serving Lee
```

tests.output:
3
Ana Max
Serving Ana
Lee to the back
Serving Max
Serving Lee

hints: Declare `bool sentBack = false;` before the loop so Lee goes to the back only once.
Inside the loop, copy the front into a `std::string` before `pop()`, then push that copy to send Lee to the back, just as the example re-queues `job`.

steps.title: std::deque: both ends
steps.body:
A `std::deque<T>` (say "deck") from `<deque>` is a double-ended queue: fast adds and removes at both ends, plus indexing like a vector.

```cpp
std::deque<int> dq = {2, 3};
dq.push_front(1);                        // add at the front
dq.push_back(4);                         // add at the back
for (int x : dq) std::cout << x << ' ';  // 1 2 3 4
std::cout << '\n';
dq.pop_front();                          // remove from the front
dq.pop_back();                           // remove from the back
std::cout << dq.front() << '\n';         // 2
std::cout << dq.back() << '\n';          // 3
std::cout << dq[1] << '\n';              // 3, random access
```

A vector's `insert` at the front shifts every element, which is O(n). A deque stores its elements in fixed-size blocks on the heap and keeps a small table of block pointers, so `push_front` just uses room in the first block or adds a new one: O(1). The cost is that elements are not one contiguous block like a vector, so `&dq[0] + i` is not a safe way to reach element `i`. Use `dq[i]`.

Because both ends are fast, `std::stack` and `std::queue` use a `std::deque` underneath by default. They are *adapters*: each wraps a container and exposes only the ends it allows. A deque is a natural fit for a sliding window: push new items on the back and pop old ones off the front.

example.title: Recently visited pages
example.prompt: Keep the last 3 visited pages in a deque, then add a page at the front and drop one from the back.
example.output:
home
home news
home news sports
news sports weather
sports weather mail
start mail
start weather
example.explanation: Each visit goes on the back. Once the size reaches 4, `pop_front()` drops the oldest page, so the window never holds more than 3. `printWindow` reads the deque by index with `window[i]`, exactly like a vector. After the loop `push_front("start")` puts a page before `sports`, so the front is `start` and the back is `mail`. `pop_back()` then removes `mail`, leaving `weather` at the back.

practice.title: Temperature window
practice.prompt:
Keep a sliding window of the last 4 temperature readings in a deque.

1. Finish `printWindow` so it prints the elements with `window[i]`, separated by single spaces.
2. For each reading, `push_back` it, `pop_front` when the size passes 4, and print the window.
3. `push_front` a baseline of `0`, then print the front and back separated by a space.
4. `pop_back` once, then print the front and back again.

Expected output:

```text
12
12 15
12 15 11
12 15 11 18
15 11 18 20
11 18 20 9
0 9
0 20
```
hints: Loop with `for (std::size_t i = 0; i < window.size(); ++i)` and print a space before every element except the first.
Check `if (window.size() > 4)` right after `push_back`, and call `pop_front()` when it is true.

steps.title: std::priority_queue: largest first

example.title: Task priorities and shortest tasks
example.prompt: Print priorities largest first with a max-heap, then tasks shortest first with a min-heap of pairs.
example.output:
9 7 3 1
call takes 5 min
email takes 5 min
review takes 15 min
report takes 25 min
example.explanation: The plain `std::priority_queue<int>` hands back 9, 7, 3, 1 no matter what order they went in. The second heap uses `std::greater<Task>`, so the smallest pair is on top. Two tasks take 5 minutes, and pairs compare by `second` on a tie, so `call` comes before `email`. `auto [minutes, name] = tasks.top();` copies the pair into two fresh variables before `pop()` removes it.

practice.title: Top scores and cheapest items
practice.prompt:
Print the three highest scores with a max-heap and the two cheapest items with a min-heap of pairs.

1. Push every score into a `std::priority_queue<int>`.
2. Pop the top 3 and print them on one line separated by single spaces.
3. Make a min-heap of `Offer` pairs and push `{4, "pen"}`, `{12, "book"}`, `{2, "eraser"}`, `{7, "ruler"}`, and `{2, "clip"}`.
4. Pop the two cheapest, copying each top with `auto [price, item]`, and print `ITEM costs PRICE` for each.

Expected output:

```text
99 91 78
clip costs 2
eraser costs 2
```
hints: Instead of draining the whole heap, use a counting for loop that pops only 3 times and still checks `!maxHeap.empty()`.
The min-heap type is `std::priority_queue<Offer, std::vector<Offer>, std::greater<Offer>>`.
Both cheapest items cost 2, so the tie is broken by name: clip before eraser.

recap:
- `std::stack<T>` from `<stack>` is last in, first out: `push`, `top`, `pop`, `empty`, `size`.
- `std::queue<T>` from `<queue>` is first in, first out: `push` at the back, `front` and `back` to read, `pop` from the front.
- `pop()` returns `void`. Copy `top()` or `front()` into a value first, never into a `const auto&`.
- `top`, `front`, `back`, and `pop` on an empty container are undefined behavior, so check `empty()`.
- `std::deque<T>` from `<deque>` adds and removes at both ends in O(1) and supports `dq[i]`.
- `std::stack` and `std::queue` are adapters over a `std::deque` by default.
- `std::priority_queue<T>` is a max-heap with O(log n) `push` and `pop`. Use `std::greater<T>` for a min-heap.
- A heap of pairs orders by `first`, then `second`: `auto [a, b] = pq.top(); pq.pop();`.
